summary: For ages 6–7: add and subtract a two-digit number and a multiple of ten (e.g. 45 + 30, 82 − 40) mentally and with concrete/pictorial support, building from '10 more/10 less'. The key insight is that adding or subtracting whole tens leaves the ones digit fixed and, while the answer stays between 0 and 99, changes only the tens digit (crossing 100, e.g. 85 + 30 = 115, also changes the hundreds). The classic error is treating the added tens as ones (45 + 30 → 48) or changing both digits. A deliberate contrast with adding ones (45 + 3) keeps the two procedures distinct.
misconceptions: Changing the ones digit as well as the tens when adding tens.
Adding the tens digit to the ones (45 + 30 → 48 or 75... e.g. treating 30 as 3 ones).
Miscounting the number of tens jumps.
For subtraction, borrowing into the ones unnecessarily.

activities.title: Add and remove tens while the ones stay put
steps: Start with a base-ten representation of 45: four ten-sticks and five single ones, with the numeral 45 shown alongside.
Before acting, predict the answer to 45 + 30 and say which digit you think will change.
Add three more ten-sticks one at a time for +30, saying the running total aloud: 45 → 55 → 65 → 75, and notice that the five single ones never move.
Switch to subtraction: start from 82 (eight ten-sticks, two ones) and remove four ten-sticks for 82 − 40, reaching 42, with the two ones untouched.

Repeat the same moves on a hundred square numbered with 1 at the top: for +30 move three rows straight down (45 → 55 → 65 → 75); for −40 move four rows straight up (82 → 72 → 62 → 52 → 42), watching that the ones column stays the same.
Immediately afterwards do 45 + 3 with single ones to feel the difference: now the ones pile changes and the tens stay the same.

Optionally, show the same tens move on other representations of place value — an empty number line with jumps of ten, a Gattegno place-value chart where the tens row slides while the ones stay, or arrow cards that separate the tens and ones — to reinforce that only the tens change.
activities.insight: Adding or subtracting a multiple of ten moves only the tens; the ones digit is invariant. Adding ones is a different move that changes the ones instead.

activities.title: Fluency practice: one-step add/subtract tens
steps: Complete fill-in items such as 45 + 30 = ___ and 82 − 40 = ___, aiming to answer in one step.
Answer 'which digit changes?' questions for an add-tens item, resisting a distractor answer that alters the ones digit.
Work through a short sequence of +10 steps (e.g. 45, 55, 65, 75) and then a −10 sequence, saying each total.
Mix in an occasional add-ones item (45 + 3) so you have to decide which digit changes each time.
activities.insight: The one-step mental move for adding/subtracting tens can become more automatic, while deliberate contrast with adding ones keeps the two procedures from merging.

activities.title: Explain and predict the invariant digit
steps: Work out 45 + 30; 82 − 40; and 45 + 3 mentally and state which digit changed each time.
Explain why only the tens change when adding or subtracting tens, and why the ones change for 45 + 3.
Predict the ones digit of 82 − 40 before calculating, then check.
Show 45 + 30 on a hundred square and describe which way you move and why.
activities.insight: Being able to articulate why the ones stay fixed (because whole tens are being added) demonstrates secure place-value reasoning beyond getting the right number.

checkQuestion: Work these out mentally and tell me which digit changed each time: 45 + 30; 82 − 40; 45 + 3.
checkAnswer: 75 (tens change, ones stay 5); 42 (tens change, ones stay 2); 48 (ones change — this one adds ONES, not tens). Watch that the child keeps the ones digit fixed when adding/subtracting tens and correctly switches to changing the ones on the last item.
